about: Source ledger of the Identity and Access Lab: every factual claim on the page, the document and section it comes from, and the date it was checked. tests/identity.test.js checks the RFC numbers and statuses against the RFC Editor.

entries.claim: 401: the request lacks valid authentication credentials; the server MUST send a WWW-Authenticate header with at least one challenge.
403: the server understood the request but refuses to fulfil it; credentials, if provided, are insufficient.
404: no current representation was found, or the server is not willing to disclose that one exists.
OAuth 2.0 lets a third-party application obtain limited access to an HTTP service, on behalf of a resource owner or on its own behalf.
OAuth defines four roles: resource owner, resource server, client, authorization server.
OpenID Connect 1.0 is a simple identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0 that lets clients verify the identity of the end-user.
entries.doc: OpenID Connect Core 1.0 incorporating errata set 2

entries.claim: SAML 2.0 is an OASIS Standard dated 15 March 2005; its most important use case is multi-domain web single sign-on, carried in XML-encoded assertions with identity provider and service provider roles.
entries.doc: OASIS SAML V2.0 (Core, OS, 15 March 2005) and the SAML V2.0 Technical Overview (committee draft 02, 25 March 2008)
entries.section: front matter; overview section on use cases

entries.claim: A JWT is a compact, URL-safe means of representing claims, encoded as a JSON object that is the payload of a JWS or the plaintext of a JWE.
A bearer token can be used by any party in possession of it, in any way another holder could; no proof of key possession is required.
PKCE mitigates the authorization code interception attack on OAuth 2.0 public clients.
TLS 1.3 allows client/server applications to communicate over the Internet in a way designed to prevent eavesdropping, tampering and message forgery; RFC 9846 obsoletes RFC 8446.
The https scheme is for an origin server capable of establishing a TLS connection secured for HTTP communication.
Internet certificates profile the X.509 v3 certificate format.
Authentication is the process of determining the validity of one or more authenticators used to claim a digital identity.
A password is "something you know"; look-up secrets and out-of-band devices are "something you have"; a biometric match serves as "something you are" (and is not an authenticator by itself).
A 403 client SHOULD NOT automatically repeat the request with the same credentials; a request might be forbidden for reasons unrelated to credentials; a server may hide a resource with 404.
Bearer is an authentication scheme: the token is sent in the Authorization header; a 401 carries a WWW-Authenticate challenge.
HMAC is a mechanism for message authentication using a cryptographic hash function in combination with a secret shared key.
Base 64 Encoding with URL and Filename Safe Alphabet replaces + and / with - and _ .
RFC 6151 updates the security considerations for MD5 and HMAC-MD5.
The first collision for full SHA-1 was produced in 2017 (received 28 February 2017).
entries.doc: Stevens, Bursztein, Karpman, Albertini, Markov: The first collision for full SHA-1, IACR ePrint 2017/190

entries.claim: A server sets a cookie with a Set-Cookie header and the browser sends it back on later requests to the same place.

Secure is sent only on https (except localhost); HttpOnly forbids document.cookie access but the cookie is still sent with script-initiated requests; SameSite Strict/Lax/None semantics; Domain omitted means host-only; __Host- requires Secure, no Domain and Path=/.
entries.doc: MDN Web Docs, Set-Cookie; RFC 6265bis draft revision 22 (4.1.3.2 and 5.6.7)

entries.claim: Lax sends same-site cookies with cross-site requests if and only if they are top-level navigations using a safe method.

Argon2id first (m=19456 KiB, t=2, p=1), then scrypt (N=2^17, r=8, p=1), bcrypt legacy (work factor 10+, 72 byte limit), PBKDF2 when FIPS-140 is required (HMAC-SHA256 600,000; HMAC-SHA512 220,000). A unique salt per password.

ASP.NET Core Identity V3 hashing: PBKDF2 with HMAC-SHA512, 128-bit salt, 256-bit subkey, 100000 iterations by default (PasswordHasherOptions.IterationCount); format marker 0x01 then prf, iteration count and salt length as 4-byte values, salt, subkey; stored base64.

Passwords used as a single factor SHALL be at least 15 characters; as part of multi-factor at least 8; verifiers SHOULD permit at least 64; no composition rules; no periodic change; compare against a blocklist; no knowledge-based questions; rate-limit failed attempts.

Session ids need at least 64 bits of entropy (128 bits for ids you make yourself, from a CSPRNG); renew the id after any privilege change; idle timeouts of 2-5 minutes (high value) or 15-30 minutes (low risk); absolute timeouts such as 4-8 hours; the server must invalidate the session at logout.

entries.claim: CSRF defences: synchronizer token, signed double-submit cookie, custom request headers, Fetch Metadata (Sec-Fetch-Site) and Origin checks; do not change state on GET; SameSite is defence in depth and does not replace a proper CSRF defence in most deployments.
entries.doc: OWASP Cross-Site Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet

entries.claim: Subdomains of one registrable domain are the same site but different origins; a subdomain takeover can enable CSRF against a cookie-based BFF, and the __Host- prefix stops the cookie being shared with subdomains.
